item.title: Source rule checks: a supplied rule, its exception and two readings carried through a checkable computation
item.description: A new engineering study in the Knowledge Contract corpus asks whether a bounded program can keep a stated rule, its exception, alternative readings and unknown facts intact while computing with them. Against a separately written oracle it matched on 16,384 and 4,096 finite cases, and a review by a non-author found one real input failure, now fixed. It is a finite check, not language understanding.
item.content:encoded:
A rule in a source often comes with an exception, and a reader may hold two readings of it. A program that computes with the rule can lose either one quietly: by clipping the exception, by merging the readings, or by treating an unknown fact as false. A study merged into the Knowledge Contract corpus on 15 November 2026 tests whether a small, bounded program keeps all three.

The question and the answer

The study, "Source Rule Checks: Finite Binding, Alternatives and Operation Composition", asks: "Can a bounded consumer preserve an explicitly supplied rule, its exception, alternative readings and unknown observations through a checkable computation?" Its input is a short authored source with NOTE and RULE lines and a supplied interpretation packet. It is explicitly "not an automatic extractor of meaning from unrestricted prose".

Each rule line must match its byte selector, its quoted text and the source digest, so a clipped prefix that drops "UNLESS suspended" is refused even when the hash of the source is valid. Unknown and withheld values both allow false and true but stay distinguishable. Every report keeps source fidelity, attribution, real-world truth and current authority as not assessed, and states that no effects are authorized.

Source: Pavel Valentov, "Source Rule Checks: Finite Binding, Alternatives and Operation Composition", Knowledge Contract engineering study, edition 1.1, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Against an oracle written separately

The expected results come from a suite that starts from Boolean truth masks and does not use the implementation's tokenizer, parser or evaluator. The study is direct about what this separation is: the oracle "was authored by a separate task from the implementation" but "shares the controller, model family and host", so it is "not external independence".

The program matched that oracle on two complete finite families:

  • all 256 Boolean functions of three variables under 64 availability profiles: 16,384 records, of which 2,952 true, 2,952 false and 10,480 undetermined;
  • all 256 ordered pairs of two-variable functions under 16 profiles: 4,096 records, with 1,088 agreements and 3,008 same-world disagreements between the two readings.

In 984 of those pair records, the two readings have the same set of possible values and still disagree in the same world. A check that compares only the sets would call them equal. The counters are checked against the declared complete inventories, so a missing function or profile cannot pass with a smaller denominator.

Source: the same study, sections "Independent expected-result method" and the finite receipt, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Where it meets the existing algebra

Four integration tests feed the program's output into the corpus's existing relation and outcome-set geometry code. One shows why aggregate distances are not enough. Two eligibility readings have the same outcome set, Hausdorff distance zero, and still disagree in two of eight common worlds. The study reads this as consistent with the stated scope of two earlier papers in the corpus, not as a counterexample to them. Another test shows that a row index of zero can carry the meaning "true", so row numbers cannot stand in for Boolean labels.

Source: the same study, section "Connection to algebra and geometry", github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

A failure that was kept

A review by a non-author sent a 5,341-byte packet containing a 5,000-digit integer in a byte selector. The packet was under the size limit, and the first implementation crashed with a Python traceback and no JSON result. The corrected reader turns such decoder errors into a structured refusal: exit 2, INVALID, malformed_json, nothing evaluated. The original module, the failed output and the corrected output are kept side by side, "the first failure was not overwritten by success". The reviewer then ran 30 further probes and found no remaining blocker within that scope, which the study states is not an exhaustive proof.

Source: the same study, section "Resolved input failure and review boundary", github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract.

Our state

Integrated: the study, its specification ("Semantic Bridge: From Source Readings to Checkable Operations", an engineering draft) and the code are on the main branch of the public Knowledge Contract repository since 15 November 2026. The review recorded for them is a review by a non-author on the same model family, not independent review.

Open, in the study's own words: general human-to-formal fidelity, quantifiers, units, time, nested attribution, required media, complete artifact integration and actual agent use. Publication decisions, index admission and native admission have separate criteria. No paid experiment was run.

Source: Knowledge Contract, merged pull request 118, github.com/Arcanada-one/knowledge-contract/pull/118.

item.title: Agent Situation: keeping a bounded view current
item.description: A new research draft examines how an agent establishes its situation, responds to change and selects context for a task. The programme separates finite controls, a planned language-model trial and eventual runtime use.
item.content:encoded:
An agent returns to a conversation with a detailed account of yesterday's work. The active account, repository revision or outcome of a pending operation may already have changed. How should it establish what is current, what remains uncertain and what matters to its next step?

Agent Situation: Initialization, Change, and Bounded Context develops this question as a research draft within Knowledge Contract's existing Agent Application programme. This article is an editorial introduction; scientific acceptance and full-text translation review remain separate work.

Begin with a partial situation

The draft proposes an initial inventory of the task, operating scope, relevant participants, available tools, ongoing operations, constraints, uncertainties and resources. Each operation selects the fields it needs. Repository maintenance may require a branch revision and build status; a physical agent may require a local reference frame and sensor observations.

Missing information stays explicit. A saved description does not establish today's account or permissions. Initialization has a bounded deadline and can support a limited response while leaving other operations unresolved. Source: research draft and engineering design.

Follow relevant changes

The proposed lifecycle connects observations to the conclusions and plans that depend on them. A changed prerequisite invalidates the affected view. A later message can contain older information, and receiving an observation again does not make it newer.

Acquisition, state updates, context selection and model calls have separate schedules. Relevant events can trigger a focused update; expiry rules provide a backstop. Conflicting observations retain their sources and scope. An uncertain external outcome calls for reconciliation before a repeated action. Source: change and refresh proposal.

Preserve the conditions needed for a decision

A model receives a selected view under a resource budget. The proposal retains declared mandatory dependencies, relevant uncertainty and an account of omissions. If required material cannot fit, the system exposes that limit and considers a smaller task or another representation.

This extends the existing Context Package vocabulary. Including a condition still leaves a further question: did the agent use it correctly? Source: bounded-context argument.

Test the proposal in separate stages

The reading record now covers 21 selected primary sources across situation awareness, context-aware systems, robotics and agent memory. Two close architectural predecessors have been added: CoALA describes persistent working memory and selected inputs for each model call; CoDRA separates context observers from robot execution. The review remains targeted. Recent preprints retain their status; Scroll contributes an abstract-level comparison, and mutable ROS documentation has recorded access dates.

The companion Context Controls study reports 21 of 21 authored finite checks passing, with all three selected disabled-guard variants detected. The initial 18 checks missed a delayed-derivation defect; review exposed it, and the correction added three controls. These are local state-model checks, with no LLM calls or real authorization mechanism. The review used agents under the same controller; external independence is not established.

A continuation review found a separate defect in the test runner: omitting one registered check let it execute only 20 of the 21 expected cases and still report success. The repair passed nine separate checks of registration completeness and result accounting. These nine checks have their own scope and count, alongside the 21 model checks and three disabled-guard variants. The state model and literal expected outcomes are unchanged, and the historical evidence is preserved.

A separate, unexecuted LLM protocol proposes comparison with a strong deterministic state manager under matched resources, measuring valid task completion, stale-value use, unnecessary refusal and total cost. Conditions 4 and 5 share the same frozen projector, optional ranking, guards and budgets; only the optional acquisition and refresh schedule changes. This comparison is designed to isolate selective refresh, while a separate benefit from projection would need its own comparison. The allocation remains 450 proposed episode-runs; none of those LLM runs have been executed. No performance gain or cost saving is reported.

Further review and a bounded pilot remain planned. The results may support a simpler deterministic design. Source: literature, finite-study scope and experiment plan.

item.title: Thirty-five gaps: a legal analysis maps DORA onto AI services, and three of them concern agents
item.description: Five authors project the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act onto AI services in finance and record 35 places where, in their reading, the rules give no criterion. Three concern agents: review by an agent in the same environment, an agent's own report, and an agent testing the system it runs. It is the authors' analysis, not a measurement, and we read only part of it.
item.content:encoded:
What does a resilience law written for IT systems say when the system is an AI service? A work published on 1 November 2026 answers for one law, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA, Regulation (EU) 2022/2554), and one sector, finance. Its answer is a list of 35 gaps, each derived by the same five steps. We read the summary, the method, the closing sections and three of the gap chains. We did not check its quotations of the law against the official texts.

What the work claims

The authors state that DORA applies to AI services without any dedicated provision, because the parts of an AI service are ICT assets and services. They note that it has been in force since 17 January 2025, and that it "regulates only ICT resilience; the correctness of AI services' decisions is not part of its subject matter".

The object they analyse is not the model. It is the AI service: the model together with what surrounds it in operation, such as data, prompts and guardrails, retrieval, the agent layer, providers, human oversight and fallback.

Across eight layers of DORA they record 35 gaps: 2 in governance, 6 in inventory and change, 4 in detection and continuity, 5 in incidents, 10 in testing, 5 in providers, 2 in oversight and 1 in information sharing. The counts are ours, taken from the table in section 2.3.

They also read the EU AI Act next to DORA. What follows is the authors' own reading in sections 13.4 and 13.5, not an official classification and not a complete one; we did not check it against the Act. In their reading, the AI Act treats as high-risk in finance only the evaluation of a person's creditworthiness and risk assessment and pricing in life and health insurance, and chatbots, internal assistants and development agents are not high-risk. For a financial entity that does use a high-risk system, they read the AI Act as counting monitoring as fulfilled through the governance rules of financial law, which rest on DORA.

Source: Yurii Chudinov, Volodymyr Tkach, Albina Dermenzhy, Dmytro Aksenov, Serhii Vatylyk, "Resilient Systems, Unverified Decisions: A Layer-by-Layer Projection of DORA onto AI Services in the EU Financial Sector", Zenodo, 1 November 2026, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

How a gap is derived

A gap is recorded only when five steps hold. One: DORA or its technical standards contain a norm that applies, shown by a verbatim quotation. Two: the norm is projected onto a specific element of the AI service. Three: a property of AI creates a failure mode the norm does not account for. Four: the norm gives no criterion, threshold or evidence for that case. Five: the consequence needs another layer of control.

The work says which steps are whose. Step one rests on a quotation. Steps two and five are marked "author's projection". If a step fails, no gap is recorded. Its example: prompt injection is specific to AI, but a data leak through it already meets the definition of an ICT-related incident, so step four fails and there is no gap.

It also limits what the word means: a gap "does not mean an automatic violation of DORA, nor does it mean an absence of regulation altogether".

This is the part closest to our subject: every conclusion says what kind of support it has, so a quoted norm and the authors' reading of it can be told apart.

Source: the same work, section 3.2, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

Three gaps about agents

We read three chains in full.

G-30. DORA's standards require that whoever approves a change is independent of whoever requests and implements it. The authors argue that changes made by AI outgrow what a person can read, so review passes to another AI, often in the same environment with shared context. The norm does not say whether such a reviewer is independent. Their remedy is to separate the reviewer's context, credentials and resources from the executor's, and to check the reviewer's conclusions against an action log.

G-31. DORA requires mechanisms to detect anomalous activity. The norm does not separate an executor's own report from evidence of its actions. For an agent, the authors write, the final answer is model output like any other and "may be incomplete or false". Detection should rely on action logs that the agent cannot modify.

G-35. DORA requires tests by independent parties. The norm is written for people and organisations and does not say whether an agent that operates a system is a party to testing it. The authors' consequence: such an agent is not admitted to testing that system.

We did not open the incident registry that the chains cite.

Source: the same work, sections 5.6, 6.6 and 8.6, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

What this changes for us, and what waits

We changed nothing because of this work. For this article we checked our own review records of 13 and 14 November, not every record we keep. In those records, a review of one agent's work by another agent is written as "a review by a non-author", and its independence is marked as not verified. In the same records, claims about a change are checked against the change itself, not against a report about it.

One thing we cannot claim. The agents in those records work under one account and with models of one family. Whether their context, credentials and resources are separated, in the sense G-30 uses, has not been verified, and we have no task for it. State: on hold.

Limits. This is a legal analysis by its authors, published on Zenodo; we saw no sign of peer review in the parts we read. It is not a measurement and not a regulator's position. We read sections 1, 2, 3, 12 to 15 and the three chains; the other 32 chains, the registries and the other files of the record are unread.

Source: the same work, doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23857406.

Also seen, not read

Two records by one of the authors were found by their metadata only. We opened no file of either. Albina Dermenzhy, "GPT Deprivation: How the Wrong Point on the Ontology and Expectations Scale Leads to Losses from Generative AI. A Multiple-Case Study, 2023–2026", doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23599162. Albina Dermenzhy, "Tech Diplomacy: A Framework for Interaction Between Probabilistic Systems, Humans, and Other Systems", doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24172092.

An article by Chuck Brooks of 24 October 2026 names the first author of the DORA work as co-founder of Compilence, which plans a hospital programme in Japan. None of the three records above mentions that programme in its metadata, description or file names. bizcatalyst360.com.

item.title: A research agent's verdict is not a test of known size
item.description: A study plants the truth in simulated data and scores what language-model research agents conclude. In simulated worlds with nothing to find, built without the repeated-value flaw of the earlier runs, three commercial research agents still claimed a finding in 34%, 16% and 44% of cases. A sentence about earlier research also changed verdicts on identical data.
item.content:encoded:
When an agent analyses data and reports that it found something, who decided that the finding is real? Usually the agent itself. A new study measures how often that decision is wrong when the right answer is known in advance. We have not reproduced it. Below is what it shows and why it matters for any rule about reusing a result.

The truth is planted, so every verdict can be scored

Chang Liu gives each agent a simulated world whose data-generating process the author controls. Most worlds are monthly return series in which one of eight candidate predictors carries a planted signal of chosen strength, or none at all; the other seven are distractors with no predictive power. The agent sees 700 months, writes and runs its own code within a budget of 40 calls, and submits a model with a verdict: the model beats a static benchmark, does not beat it, or the search is abandoned. A further 360 months never enter the agent's sandbox and are used only to evaluate what it submitted.

Because the truth is known by construction, the agent can be treated like any statistical test. Two quantities matter. Size is how often it claims a finding in a world without a signal. Power is how often it detects a signal that is there. The author scores the verdict against the conventional 5% level, although the brief names no level: which threshold the agent applies on its own is one of the things measured.

Source: Chang Liu, "Are LLM Research Agents Reliable Judges of Predictability? Evidence from Planted-Signal Worlds", arXiv:2611.04070v1.

A finding was reported where there was nothing to find

In the first two studies, three commercial models claimed predictability in 21%, 19% and 63% of the worlds without a signal. An external review then found a flaw in the worlds: resampled shock values repeated exactly, so a lookup of past returns could forecast even an empty world, and the model with the highest rate exploited it. A third study replaced those shocks with Gaussian ones. The rates became 34%, 16% and 44%, and each model still claimed more often than a conventional test run on the same worlds. An open-weight model that runs on one workstation claimed in 35% of the empty worlds, and its rate barely rose when a signal was planted.

The agent of the first study did detect weak signals more often than a conventional out-of-sample test. The author's explanation is that it accepts weaker evidence. Held to the same false-positive rate, a conventional in-sample test with a correction for multiple candidates detected weak signals about as often, and more often than the model with the highest false-claim rate.

The stated confidence added little. In all 3,990 runs of the three commercial models, the agent claimed a finding exactly when its stated probability was at least one half. In the author's words, the implicit rule is a 50% posterior, not a 5% test.

Source: Chang Liu, the same paper, sections 1, 4 to 5 and 7.1, arXiv:2611.04070v1.

One sentence about prior research moved the verdict

In the first study, 160 worlds were run three times with the same data and one sentence changed at the end of the brief: nothing, a remark that prior research found a signal, or a remark that it found none. The share of worlds in which the agent claimed a finding was 32% under the sceptical sentence, 46% under the neutral brief and 61% under the optimistic one. The verdict differed between framings in 50 of the 160 worlds. In the worlds without a signal, the optimistic sentence raised false claims from 15% to 32%. In the worlds with a signal, the sceptical sentence lowered detection from 56% to 40%.

Source: Chang Liu, the same paper, section 3.3, arXiv:2611.04070v1.

What the author recommends, and where the evidence stops

The protocol the paper proposes is short: give a neutral brief; let the agent build the model but not issue the verdict; fix the decision rule in advance, outside the agent; keep the holdout technically out of its reach. The author says plainly that the last item is enforced by his harness and was not tested as a factor.

A sealed holdout is not free. In an exploratory analysis of the models the agents submitted in the third study, a holdout test at the 5% level claimed in at most 5% of the empty worlds, but for the three commercial models it detected only 25% to 28% of the worlds whose planted signal explains 1% of the variance, against 54% for the in-sample test. The author therefore treats the holdout as confirmation and an efficient pre-specified test as the primary rule.

The limits are stated in the paper. One agent configuration, one tool set and one brief were studied. The worlds are stylised: one planted predictor among eight. The false-positive rate that anchors the matched comparisons rests on 40 worlds. Two of the models were served under names without dated snapshots. The pre-specifications were recorded in repository commits, not in a public registry, and several of the stronger comparisons were designed after the first results were known.

What this means for our work. Knowledge Contract asks when a result may be relied on by someone who did not produce it. This study gives a measured reason to keep two roles apart: the one who searches and the one who decides, with the deciding rule written down before the search starts. It also shows that a stated probability is not evidence of calibration. We have not run such an experiment ourselves. A comparison on synthetic cases with and without a planted effect, scored by a rule fixed beforehand, has been proposed inside our research intake and is on hold: no owner has accepted it and no work has started.

Source: Chang Liu, the same paper, sections 7.1 and 7.2, arXiv:2611.04070v1.

item.title: Before crediting the context, control for the topic
item.description: A paper shows that a standard test of personalised memory mostly measures topic match. What that means for any claim that selected knowledge helped, and one audit of our own that moved from proposal to the main branch.
item.content:encoded:
Knowledge Contract is about what an agent may rely on. A neighbouring question is how anyone shows that the knowledge an agent was given actually helped. One paper this week takes apart a common way of showing it. We also report a change of state in our own work.

The wrong-user test measures the topic

Karina Romanova, Igor Kiselev, Vladimir Platonov, Viliana Devbunova, Gregory Leleytner, Adeliya Leleytner, Lina Veltman and Aleksandr Nikolich examine a test that is widely used for personalised models. Give the model a user's own history, then replace it with another user's history, and measure how far accuracy drops. The drop is read as proof that the model uses what it knows about this person.

The authors point out that the swap changes two things. The other user wrote about other subjects, so the history stops matching the topic of the question as well as the person. They separate the two on a news categorisation task (LaMP-2) with a frozen language model, using histories of similar users and synthetic histories assembled from other users' articles. The measure throughout is accuracy of the predicted category.

The user's own history improves accuracy by 2.3 percentage points over a model trained without any history. If history is removed only at evaluation, from a model trained with it, the same gain appears as 4.8 points. Category labels alone reproduce 86% of the accuracy gap between the user's own history and a random user's history. When the synthetic history is matched on labels and on text similarity, the gap falls to 0.9 points. Across two user splits and three training seeds, the advantage of the own history over a similar user's history is 3.2 points for users seen in training and 0.65 points for unseen users, and the authors call the evidence for the latter inconclusive.

The limits are theirs: one main task, a small model, and a second experiment on movie tags with a single training seed. Whether the result holds for larger models and other tasks is not shown.

What this means for Knowledge Contract. Replace "the user's history" with "the context selected for this task" and the same trap is open. If an agent does better with selected knowledge than with a random document, part of the gain is that the selected text is about the right subject. That says little about whether the admitted, scoped, evidenced knowledge was the cause. A claim of benefit needs two comparisons the paper names: a control of similar content that is not the selected knowledge, and a baseline that was set up to work without the context, not one that had it taken away at test time.

Our state: on hold. The control design is recorded in our research roadmap as a requirement for any future benefit claim. We have not measured a benefit of context selection, with or without this control, and we have not reproduced the paper. The return condition is a concrete, measurable claim that selection helped.

Source: Karina Romanova, Igor Kiselev, Vladimir Platonov, Viliana Devbunova, Gregory Leleytner, Adeliya Leleytner, Lina Veltman, Aleksandr Nikolich. Not Your Diary, Just Your Topic: Grading the Wrong-User Control. arXiv:2611.09609v1, 6 November 2026.

The audit of the first premise is now on the main branch

Yesterday we described an audit of one of our propositions as an open proposal. It concerns a chain of transformations: if a property holds at the start and each step preserves it under stated conditions at the joins, it holds at the end. The audit asked what is lost if the starting premise is dropped.

That proposal was merged on 11 November. It is worth being exact about what the merge contains. It adds an audit note, ten finite test cases and a workflow that runs them in continuous integration. One case is a small witness showing that without the starting premise the conclusion can fail. Four two-step cases separate the two conditions at the joins from each other. The merge does not amend the proposition and does not prove it by enumeration; the text of the paper is unchanged. A later increment in the same change tightened the accounting of the tests themselves, so that the workflow checks which cases were actually selected and executed and does not rely on a count of definitions.

We did not re-run the cases for this article; the description follows the merged change itself.

Source: Knowledge Contract, "C03 scientific audit: preserve initial-state premise in chain observation theorem", knowledge-contract #98, merged 11 November 2026.

What comes next

The two items meet in one rule. A statement that something holds, or helps, has to name what it was compared with and what was assumed at the start. For the proposition, the starting premise is now guarded by tests. For context selection, the comparison does not exist yet, and until it does we make no claim of benefit.

item.title: A lesson without its evidence ages first
item.description: Two new papers on agent memory and reuse of experience, one theorem tested by removing its first premise, and one rule we drew from our own mistake. The Knowledge Contract week in review.
item.content:encoded:
Knowledge Contract answers one question: what is an agent entitled to rely on, and why. This week two independent research groups asked the same question, and we found two flaws in our own checks. Below: both papers, one audit of a theorem and one new rule.

Memory helps as long as you can go back to the source

Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek and Sung Ju Hwang study an awkward property of agent memory: a stored lesson sometimes makes the agent worse at tasks it used to solve without it. Their system, WikiTrace, keeps each lesson together with its conditions of applicability, the outcome of the episode and the original trace. The agent receives the lessons up front and descends to the evidence when details are missing, lessons contradict each other, or an action has failed.

Across eight task sets the average score was 90.2, against 87.0 for the same lessons without evidence and 79.5 with no memory at all. Regressions on previously solvable tasks fell from 6.5% to 4.5%. The price: 1.17 times the run-time spend.

The authors state their limits plainly and we repeat them. The comparison changes two things at once, access to evidence and the instruction given to the agent, so the share of each is unknown. The corpora are small, 38 to 54 training tasks. An average over dissimilar sets cannot be read as a fraction of tasks solved.

What this means for Knowledge Contract. We already keep the chain of statement, source, revision and check; a second memory store is not needed. What was missing is a rule for when an agent must descend from a short lesson to its evidence. Our research review proposes four grounds: the scope of applicability is unclear; the schema or the state of the environment has changed; two lessons contradict each other; the expected action has already failed. And one limit: reading the evidence does not confirm the lesson and does not revive an expired permission. Authority is checked separately, every time.

We have put a separate system on hold until the first measured regression caused by a lesson.

Source: Yukyeong Lee, Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, Sung Ju Hwang. Don't Just Trust Your Memory: Evidence-Linked Memory Reduces Memory-Induced Degradation in LLM Agents. arXiv:2611.14320v1, 10 November 2026.

A procedure can be turned into code. Whether it should be is the question

Kaiyuan Hou, Yang Ping Kuo, Indranil Bhattacharya, Rohith Nama, Arushi Gupta, Carlos D. Castillo, Prathap Ramachandra, Xiaofan Jiang and Francesco Carbone propose ReTrace: conditions are extracted from a procedure description and agent traces, ordinary code is generated from them, and an unknown state halts execution.

The authors used 79 internal procedures, but each method was scored only on the procedures it could run: ReTrace on 77, the planning agent on 76, plain few-shot code generation on 70. Averaged over procedures, the platform marked 93.8% of ReTrace executions as finished, at 0.096 dollars per task; 96.8% for the agent, at 0.127 dollars; 88.6% for few-shot generation, at 0.033 dollars. The authors warn that the platform can mark a failed run as finished, so these are completion marks, not verified results.

The third line is the one that matters. The cheapest option costs about a third as much, and its completion mark is 5.2 points lower. The two were scored on different sets of procedures, so that gap describes the published figures; it is not a head-to-head result. Any elaborate scheme has to beat it under equal conditions before it is worth discussing. For us this becomes a requirement on future specifications: every branch of a procedure needs observable preconditions, the origin of its inputs, a test and a route for the unknown state. An explanation generated by a model stays a hypothesis and grants no authority.

Adoption is on hold until we have a stable, repeated procedure with a measured cost.

Source: Kaiyuan Hou, Yang Ping Kuo, Indranil Bhattacharya, Rohith Nama, Arushi Gupta, Carlos D. Castillo, Prathap Ramachandra, Xiaofan Jiang, Francesco Carbone. ReTrace: Distilling Tool-Using Agents into Planner-Free Workflows. arXiv:2611.14492v1, 10 November 2026.

What a theorem loses without its first premise

A scientific audit of our corpus examined the chain observation theorem. The theorem states its first premise explicitly: the chain begins in a state that satisfies the precondition of the first step. The audit asked what happens if a reader drops that premise, which is a tempting shortcut. It built a finite countermodel: without the premise the stronger conclusion is false. The theorem itself is neither refuted nor amended. The audit is published as an open proposal and is under separate scientific review; it is not yet accepted.

The instructive part was checking the check. The first countermodel had a single step. With one step, the junction conditions between steps hold trivially: there are no junctions. The tests passed and said nothing about either junction premise. The suite now includes two-step models in which a junction premise actually fires, and for each premise a case where violating it breaks the result.

The second finding is simpler and more embarrassing. Six tests sat in the repository, the build was green, and the build never ran them. A dedicated build job runs them now, ten cases in all, and we read its log: which command, how many tests, how many skipped.

Source: Knowledge Contract, proposal "C03 scientific audit: preserve initial-state premise in chain observation theorem" — knowledge-contract #98

One fact, seven places

The engineering week began with something small: the inventory of translations did not match reality. Fixing it took four rounds of review. The cause was the same each time: one fact was written in several places and they were edited one at a time. The inventory now distinguishes 31 current files, 30 historical and 34 planned.

A rule grew out of this. It is written into the new revision of the scientific role's working procedure, which is under review. Before changing a fact, list every place where it is stated or consumed: source, register, catalogue, heading, translation, checking script, site. Change them together, or record explicitly who changes the rest and when. Historical records are not rewritten.

Source: Knowledge Contract, correction of the translation inventory — knowledge-contract #97

What comes next

The updated materials will appear on the site once the build has been verified. We reproduced none of the external results; all figures belong to their authors. These briefings will appear every morning.
